https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: The five surviving panels of Antonello’s Polittico di San Gregorio – three of which were stolen on Saturday. Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/Reuters View image in fullscreen The five surviving panels of Antonello’s Polittico di San Gregorio – three of which were stolen on Saturday. Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/Reuters Art Rare Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museum Four works were taken during public holiday, the day after Italian police recovered paintings by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse Lorenzo Tondo in Palermo Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.42 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 08.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Four of the most important works of art by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina. Thieves gained access to the regional museum of Messina , or MuMe, on Saturday evening, possibly capitalising on attention being focused on La Vara, a huge religious festival that takes place in the city on 15 August, when Italy marks the ferragosto national holiday. Bypassing the alarm systems, the gang broke into a security display box and stole four wood panels painted by Antonello. View image in fullscreen The fourth, smaller stolen work, which depicts Virgin and Child. Photograph: Museo Regionale Accascina Messina/Reuters Thieves took three of the five surviving panels that made up an altarpiece known as the Polittico di San Gregorio , one of the Sicilian painter’s most important works. Originally composed of six panels created for the Monastero di San Gregorio, which was destroyed in the 1908 Messina earthquake, the altarpiece was the only work by the Sicilian painter never to have left his home city. A fourth work was taken from a secure display case: a small double-sided painting depicting the Virgin and Child with a Franciscan monk on one side and Christ on the other. The painting had belonged to the Wilhelm Soldan collection and was sold by Christie’s to the Sicilian regional government in 2003, the year it was attributed to Antonello. Born around ​1430, Antonello trained in Naples where he studied the works of Provençal and Flemish artists, whose influence is apparent in his works. In February, the Italian government secured a rare Antonello masterpiece at auction in New York, spending $14.9m (£11m) on his Ecce Homo . The painting, sold at Sotheby’s, is an intensely human portrait of the suffering Christ , believed to have been completed about 1460. The theft took place after Italian police on Friday had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were stolen earlier this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma. https://www.bursa.ro/experts-maintain-th.text: Romanian neurosurgery is at a level comparable to that of Western countries, and several clinics in Romania possess advanced medical technologies, according to Prof. Dr. Adrian Bălaşa, Head of the Neurosurgery Clinic at the Târgu-Mureş County Emergency Clinical Hospital and President of the Romanian Society of Neurosurgery (SRN). This statement was made in Braşov during the opening of the 51st Congress of the Romanian Society of Neurosurgery, an event attended by over 230 specialists from four continents. *Romanian clinics equipped with state-of-the-art technology "There is nothing in Western countries that we do not also have," stated Prof. Dr. Adrian Bălaşa, referring to the current state of neurosurgery in Romania. According to him, the field is constantly modernizing through the development of new medical facilities. Examples include the recently inaugurated center in Cluj and the Burn Center in Târgu-Mureş, where four of the 25 operating rooms are dedicated exclusively to neurosurgery. Both centers, he noted, benefit from state-of-the-art technology. "The Romanian Society of Neurosurgery is involved in education - particularly for young professionals - and in bringing the latest global trends and scientific advancements to Romania, ensuring that patients here benefit from the latest knowledge and innovations worldwide," the SRN president stated. He emphasized that neurosurgery is "the most technology-driven branch of surgery" and that the use of new technologies can help improve the medical services provided to patients. *Investments do not yet cover the entire country However, Prof. Dr. Adrian Bălaşa acknowledged that investments in state-of-the-art technology are not currently distributed across all regions of the country. He believes that equipment should be prioritized for clinics that treat patients from across the country, handle a complex range of pathologies, and possess the necessary human resources. "You cannot invest in clinics where the necessary human resources are lacking," he stated. The President of the Romanian Society of Neurosurgery noted that the organization has provided the Ministry of Health with a strategy for the field's development. Additionally, last year saw the creation of the first treatment guideline for stroke, based on protocols established by the Romanian National Stroke Association and the Romanian Society of Neurology. The guideline includes intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke. *Guideline for standardizing stroke treatment According to Prof. Dr. Bălaşa, the guideline aims to standardize the treatment of patients with ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes, ensuring they have comparable chances of survival and recovery regardless of the region where they are located. "Wherever in the country such a misfortune might strike, you should receive the same treatment and have equal chances of survival and a life after the event," he explained. He noted that the strategy's implementation also depends on decisions made by the authorities, while specialists seek to support these measures through their expertise and institutional efforts. "There is a clear trend toward modernization in Romania generally, and in neurosurgery specifically. Of course, these investments do not cover the entire country; they must be directed primarily to centers that treat patients from across Romania and handle complex medical conditions," stated the SRN president. Dr. Cristian Kakucs, Head of the Neurosurgery Department at the Braşov County Emergency Clinical Hospital, stated that the unit currently treats a wide range of conditions, with a team of six physicians. He noted that the department's growth has been supported by investments in equipment and the establishment of a permanent on-call service. "We are constantly developing, partly because the authorities have recognized the importance of advancing this field; furthermore, given that Braşov is a tourist destination, we see many foreign nationals and handle a high volume of emergency cases," Dr. Kakucs said. According to him, the department strives to maintain international standards and address the broadest possible spectrum of medical conditions. Currently, the department treats craniocerebral and vertebromedullary trauma, brain tumors, and hydrocephalus. Dr. Kakucs added that some patients choose other medical centers due to a lack of up-to-date information regarding the level of development at the Braşov County Emergency Clinical Hospital. *Cluj: A Training Hub for Sub-specializations The former president of the Romanian Society of Neurosurgery, Prof. Dr. Ioan Ştefan Florian - head of the Neurosurgery Clinic in Cluj - emphasized. This highlights the importance of developing high-performance centers for physician training as well. He announced that the newly inaugurated center in Cluj will enable the training of neurosurgeons across all sub-specialties, including fully trained physicians seeking further specialization. "We look forward to welcoming as many residents as possible. We recently opened the new center in Cluj - a facility representing a unique concept within Europe, I might add - where we will be able to train neurosurgeons in all sub-specialties, including qualified physicians wishing to pursue advanced specialization," stated Prof. Dr. Ioan Ştefan Florian. He also expressed hope that Braşov would develop a neurosurgeon training center with the support of Transilvania University. Articol despre Medicine, specializations, neurosurgery, facilities.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Drone shots of new mega-warehouse in Astley Greater Manchester ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression Josh Halliday North of England editor Mon 9 Nov 2026 02.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home. “It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester . Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”. Andy Burnham expressed concern over the development weeks before he became prime minister, and Bev Craig, his successor as Greater Manchester mayor, said she too was concerned. “Old industry wouldn’t have got that close to your house,” she said. “So why is it that new industry can?” This week, villagers will attempt to block plans by Whistl, the distribution firm that operates the warehouse, to use dozens of HGVs and trailers for its round-the-clock operation. In a two-day public inquiry, they will describe how the “cacophony” of noise is already driving some to sleep deprivation and depression. “It’s had a profound impact on the neighbourhood,” said Retford, a burly man with a booming voice who after so many years in the police is not easily shaken. “The noise wakes you up at 2am and you can’t get back to sleep. We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year. It’s a living hell.” View image in fullscreen A warehouse towers over residential properties in Astley. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian This once-quiet village is now on the frontline in a nationwide fightback against superstructures springing up everywhere from Devon to Cardiff and the Scottish Borders . Plans were announced last week for Britain’s largest datacentre at the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire, and a further 315 “hyperscale” datacentres are queueing to connect to the National Grid. Down the road from Retford’s house, a woman looked out of her daughter’s bedroom window at the Whistl warehouse just metres away. The woman, a police officer who does not want to be named, said her 10-year-old son, who is autistic, refused to play in the garden because of the “continuously whirring” noise of the conveyor belts. Her eight-year-old daughter has become too scared to play in her bedroom. “As soon as she comes home from school, those blinds will be shut because she doesn’t want anyone to see in,” she said, pointing to a CCTV camera on the warehouse facing their home. “She hates it. She does get scared about it.” Like many of their neighbours, the woman and her husband moved to Astley before plans had been submitted by a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, run by the billionaire John Whittaker. View image in fullscreen Stephen Retford in his back garden: ‘We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year.’ Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Back then, they were surrounded by farmland where lambs, cows and horses grazed. Now their view is a giant hunk of grey steel that was named the worst new building in the UK this year. “It was a lovely view, so secluded,” she said. “When we saw the structure of this, it was like: oh my God, what is this?” As mayor, Burnham said earlier this year that the development had not been managed properly and that key things “should have been done differently”. Wigan council said it acted properly in approving the superstructure despite objections from the local MP and dozens of residents. However, the council’s leader, Labour’s Nazia Rehman, admitted last month that “some lessons have been learned” and said that in future “consultations [with residents] will be proactive”. Local leaders have scrapped plans for four other giant warehouses in response to the backlash. Helen Halbous, who moved to the estate seven years ago, said: “It’s a feeling of being screwed over by Wigan council, having been born and brought up here. People who had a voice of power [in the council] either made this awful decision or they looked away and let it happen. It was a little mining village and now we’re this industrial centre. It’s so wrong.” View image in fullscreen Helen Halbous moved to the estate seven years ago. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The view from Halbous’s back window. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Halbous, 47, said she and her partner, Sami Halbous, now felt trapped in a house they once loved and they feared they would be unable to sell up. “A neighbour had their home valued and they lost 30%, and that’s if they can sell,” she said. Residents felt hoodwinked about the size of the structure and its closeness to their homes, Halbous said. “The plan in 2019 was it was to be used for employment. It was never to have an 18-metre-high warehouse. Those permissions were changed [before 2024] and changed really quietly. We wouldn’t have bought here and let ourselves get trapped like this.” PLP, the land owner, said the size and scale of the buildings had not changed since its planning application in 2023. It said earlier plans for smaller units, submitted in 2017 by Peel, one of its biggest shareholders, had since lapsed. Wigan council said it recognised the “strength of feeling in the community and do not underestimate the impact residents tell us the development has had on them”. It said an independent review found its planning process was “legally sound” and followed national guidelines but there were “lessons around engagement and transparency”. It said: “We have acknowledged those findings and have taken steps to improve our approach.” View image in fullscreen A Whistl lorry arriving at the Astley business park. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Whistl, which began operating at the site in July, has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles and stopping their use outside between midnight and 6am. The firm said it took residents’ concerns seriously and was “committed to meeting its licensing responsibilities and being a good neighbour”. A Whistl spokesperson said the noise mitigation measures would remain in place and the overnight pause on activity in the yard would continue while all parties tried to “identify a sustainable, long-term solution”. Retford became so fed up with the disturbance that he began overnight observations to track the big vehicles clanking around near his home. He commissioned independent acoustics experts to produce a sound report, convinced that the “cacophony of rolling thunder, a booming sound”, breached regulations. View image in fullscreen Residents have complained of a ‘cacophony’ of noise. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian A fightback fund launched by residents has so far raised £78,000 , much of which will be spent on lawyers for next week’s public inquiry. For Retford and his wife, Carole, 71, the impact has been huge. “Bloody hell, there’s not a lot of things I’ve not seen in my life,” he said. “I don’t get easily shocked and I’m not a flaky character, but this has had a profound effect on me. We’re not fuddy-duddies or nimbies. This is big business riding over the little people like us, saying ‘screw the lot of you’.” Retford and his wife have spoken to their doctor about sleep deprivation. “It’s a torture for a very good reason, because it just drains you – and that is the effect it’s having on us,” he said. Carole became close to tears. Staring up at the warehouse, she said: “It’s changed our lives. Your moods go up and down to being very depressed and very emotional about it because there’s no way out at the minute . People use the ‘depression’ word too lightly, but if you feel there’s no way out, it does get to you.” Explore more on these topics Greater Manchester Communities Local government Planning policy Couriers/delivery industry North of England England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Ilse Aigner has been nominated by the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, as his candidate for the German presidency. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA View image in fullscreen Ilse Aigner has been nominated by the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, as his candidate for the German presidency. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA Germany ‘The time is ripe’: ex-helicopter engineer poised to be Germany’s first female president Backed by MPs from across the political divide, Bavarian Ilse Aigner offers an approachability and warmth the chancellor lacks Kate Connolly in Berlin Fri 13 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 00.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google G ermany has had 12 presidents since the end of the second world war, all of them men. Now, for the first time, the federal republic is on the brink of getting a female head of state. But Ilse Aigner, the lead candidate for the post, is unusual in more ways than one. “No law degree. No marriage. No penis,” is how the left-leaning Taz newspaper put it this week – a wry, if blunt, assessment of what a break with history the 61-year-old Bavarian represents. Friedrich Merz, Germany’s Christian Democrat (CDU) chancellor, put Aigner forward as his candidate this week after months of speculation, saying it was “high time” a woman took up the role. If elected in January, Aigner will succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier in what is a largely ceremonial role but nonetheless Germany’s highest state position. And as she has the backing not only of Merz’s CDU but his Social Democrat partners and the opposition Greens, little is standing in her way. Some are delighted. Jörg Thadeusz, a liberal writer and popular TV presenter with a penchant for satire, has taken his enthusiasm for Aigner so far as to have the name Ilse tattooed on his upper left arm. Pictures of him revealing the tattoo on TV this week made headline news, as media talked of the Aigner-Welle (Aigner wave) to describe the unexpected ripple of enthusiasm for the Catholic Bavarian – among the political establishment, at least. ‘A candidate who right now could really do Germany some good,’ said the TV presenter Jörg Thadeuzs, revealing his ‘Ilse’ tattoo. Photograph: RTL/ntv “Ilse Aigner is … a candidate who right now could really do Germany some good,” said Thadeusz. Unlike far-right populists who were polarising the country with their demands for “Deutschland First”, he said, Aigner embraced a form of Heimat (homeland) that was “neither folklore nor a political battle cry”. Not everyone shares his enthusiasm. Aigner’s relationship with the populist Alternative für Deutschland, the largest opposition force in the Bundestag, got off to a tricky start this week after she turned down their demand to present herself to them as a candidate. Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader and the most prominent woman in German politics, accused Aigner of failing to respect “democratic culture and manners” as well as “the millions of voters we represent”. View image in fullscreen Aigner, then the agriculture minister, with the then chancellor, Angela Merkel, in 2016. She entered the Bundestag in 1998. Photograph: Michaela Rehle/Reuters Despite having held a cabinet position, as agriculture minister from 2008 to 2013 under Angela Merkel, Aigner is not a household name. She began in local politics 30 years ago and entered the Bundestag in 1998. Instead of the usually prerequisite degree, she has a vocational qualification as an electrical engineer with a speciality in manufacturing helicopters, her job before entering politics. “She’s the first head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany who can personally repair a government helicopter,” Thadeusz quipped this week. In her nomination speech this week, Aigner said she hoped to inspire aspirational Germans: “As the first woman in the highest state office, I would stand with my person and my background as a symbol of the promise of upward mobility in our country.” Aigner has spoken openly about surviving two serious tumour diagnoses – one in her spinal cord when she was 17, and thyroid cancer in her 40s, when she was a minister – saying they had given her perspective as a politician. Now feted by the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to the CDU, she once struggled to be recognised. Her attempts in the early 90s, aged 27, to become mayor of her birth town, Feldkirchen-Westerham, south-east of Munich, failed because she was unmarried, which the party of arch-conservatives said was “too unclear a condition” and made her unsuitable to serve. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion She still lives in Feldkirchen-Westerham, a Bavarian town of 10,000 people, where her parents ran an electronics shop. There she shares a house on a 1970s estate living under one roof with three generations of her family, including her three older sisters and their offspring. Local people refer to her affectionally as “ die Ilse ” (equivalent to “the Ilse”, or “our Ilse”), and describe her as being a regular attender at town celebrations. She typically cycles, “whether to the butchers and bakers, or to the opening of a new windfarm”, one resident said. View image in fullscreen ‘Her approach compensates for what Merz lacks,’ wrote one Munich paper. Photograph: Annegret Hilse/Reuters For Merz the chance to back the first female presidency is a chance to shed his reputation as a Frauenfeind (misogynist), an image that goes back in part to his decades-long rivalry with Merkel, but has been underscored to some extent by his leadership style in office. In an editorial this week, the Münchner Merkur noted that Aigner’s perceived strengths neatly complemented the chancellor’s deficiencies: “Her approach compensates for what Merz lacks: approachability, popularity, a warmth that can absorb the effects of polarisation.” Merkel was regarded as a powerful female trailblazer not just in Germany but around the world. She was referred to at home as “Mutti” – both a term of affection and patronisingly used to describe her supposedly maternal stewardship of the country. Five years after her departure from the political stage, feminist commenters hope Aigner might prove a symbolic boost. “The time is ripe for a woman. We have such an under-representation of women in society, in politics, in business, and it’s high time a woman held this highest office in the land. I’m very happy about that,” said Britta Hasselmann, a leading Green MP, in a podcast interview this week. But even more important, Hasselmann emphasised, was the extent to which Aigner might draw together a country deeply divided by ideological rifts and economic tensions, where extremists are snapping at the heels of the political centre. The presidency needed someone “who can unite people, especially in such polarised times, who is empathetic, down to earth, and who tries to send a strong signal that common ground is valued in a democracy. And I believe she is capable of that,” Hasselmann said. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-m.text: PARIS — Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said she would be prepared to hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, in the wake of her promises to stop French financial aid to Ukraine. Speaking on the sidelines of a trade fair in Paris, Le Pen said a meeting in Brussels would be “justified” because “the topic of Ukraine financing is rattling Europe.” “The German chancellor is starting to threaten people, it’s starting to be an issue in Europe and it would be interesting to discuss this,” she said in a reference to Friedrich Merz’s threats to cut EU funds for countries who refuse to support Ukraine financially. Advertisement Advertisement Le Pen said she would offer to hold talks with Zelenskyy when she meets the Ukrainian ambassador in France on Monday. The far-right leader is the front-runner ahead of next year’s presidential election and has repeatedly said France can no longer afford to keep financing Ukraine’s war effort. She has estimated that French aid amounts to €6 billion per year, a figure Zelenskyy has challenged. He said the military partnership with Paris is “a win-win” relationship. Zelenskyy also invited Le Pen to Kyiv, telling French weekly l’Express that Le Pen would “change her mind” if she met Ukrainians. Financial aid to Ukraine has become an issue in next year’s presidential election amid difficult budget negotiations. This month far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon also courted controversy when he said that a post-war referendum on the future of the Donbas should be held in the area, which is mostly under Russian occupation.
